statements.text: I believe the light-touch approach the United States has taken on internet regulation is a good model to follow for AI. The explosive growth of internet innovation in our country is in large part a result of government not weighing down a new technology with heavy-handed regulation.

Before I close, I do want to mention one troubling thing among the good news about the regular-order process, and that is the Democrat leader's decision, in his words, to ``invent a new process'' to deal with the thorny question of regulating AI, or artificial intelligence, because the committee process ``won't suffice''—``won't suffice.''
statements.context: Senate floor remarks during executive session on the regular-order appropriations process, where Thune raises objections to the Majority Leader's approach to AI regulation.

statements.text: The FTC has indicated it may regulate emerging technologies like artificial intelligence. And the question I have is, do you believe the FTC has the authority to regulate AI or should it be left to Congress?
statements.context: Senate hearing on nominations to the FTC and CPSC, where Senator Thune questions a nominee about AI regulatory authority.

statements.text: Well, and let me just say, I have serious concerns about the FTC regulating or making any attempt to regulate AI. [...] But rather than having the heavy handed regulations from agencies like the FTC that I think in many cases stifle innovation in this emerging space, I have been working with my colleagues up here on both sides of the aisle to develop a light touch approach that avoids the unnecessary Government intervention that so that innovation can continue to flourish.
statements.context: Senate hearing on nominations to the FTC and CPSC, where Senator Thune questions a nominee and outlines his preferred approach to AI oversight.

statements.text: I am focused on ensuring that the Senate puts the necessary guardrails in place while also ensuring that any legislation encourages and not stifles innovation in AI.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee oversight hearing on CHIPS and Science Act implementation, featuring Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo.

statements.text: there is a bipartisan bill that I am working on that is focused on putting the right guardrails in place for the highest impact AI systems while also, at the same time, allowing for innovation.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in agriculture, Senator Thune questioning a witness about AI guardrails and strategic competition.

statements.text: This Act may be cited as the ``Artificial Intelligence Research, Innovation, and Accountability Act of 2023''.
statements.context: Senate floor introduction of S. 3312 by Senator Thune, who asked unanimous consent to print the full bill text in the Congressional Record.

statements.text: AI is a revolutionary technology that has the potential to improve health care, agriculture, logistics and supply chains, and countless other industries. As this technology continues to evolve, we should identify some basic rules of the road that protect consumers, foster an environment in which innovators and entrepreneurs can thrive, and limit government intervention.
statements.venue: Press release on AI Research, Innovation, and Accountability Act

statements.text: Our bill focuses on two things: transparency for consumers and a tiered, risk-based framework for oversight of the highest impact applications of AI. On the transparency front, our bill would require any large-scale internet platform that uses generative AI to create content to clearly inform consumers of that fact. One of the risks presented by generative AI is the difficulty distinguishing AI-produced content from human-produced content.
statements.context: Senate floor speech introducing bipartisan AI legislation (the Artificial Intelligence Research, Innovation, and Accountability Act) during an executive session on artificial intelligence.

statements.text: I see transparencies I mentioned as the key to ensuring that both developers and deployers of AI systems are accountable to the consumers and businesses they serve. [...] could you expound just briefly on what constitutes a deployer versus a developer as well as explain how obligations for developers and deployers differ when it comes to transparency and accountability?
statements.context: Senate hearing remark on AI transparency, asking a witness to clarify regulatory roles.

statements.text: But this notion—this data that came out by the Department of Justice that it had dismantled a Russian bot farm intended to sow discord in the United States and that the AI—the Russians created scores of fictitious profiles and then generated these posts. [...] the AI accelerant on the bot system makes it an imperative.
statements.context: Senate hearing or floor discussion on privacy and AI, referencing a DOJ takedown of a Russian bot farm.

statements.text: The bill establishes a framework to bolster innovation while bringing greater transparency, accountability, and security to the development and operation of the highest impact applications of AI. [...] Through this legislation basic safety and security guardrails are established for the highest risk applications of AI without requiring a burdensome audit or stamp of approval from the government, and it is my hope the Committee will advance the legislation soon.
statements.context: Opening remarks at a Senate Commerce Committee hearing on privacy and AI.

statements.text: I also mentioned, and you have talked about it already, alluded to artificial intelligence, but I believe we need to craft a legislative framework that provides basic accountability for high-risk AI models without onerous regulations.
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce, where Senator Thune outlines his AI regulatory priorities.

statements.text: As we compete to be the leader in artificial intelligence, Mr. Lutnick agrees that we should use the tried-and-true light-touch approach that has enabled the United States to lead in the digital era. [...] I am glad that the Trump administration has committed to American leadership in AI and the Commerce Department will have a critical role to play in balancing accountability with AI's great possibilities.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by John Thune supporting the nomination of Howard Lutnick as Secretary of Commerce.

statements.text: The boom in data center construction – in particular to power the rise of artificial intelligence – is placing, and will place, vast new demands upon the grid.
We want to be the leaders in AI and quantum and all these new technologies. And the way to do that is not to come in with a heavy hand of government, it's to come in with a light touch,

It needs to strike a balance, light touch. You don’t want to stifle innovation but you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated. [...] There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race, which I also think is very important.
statements.venue: Remarks to reporters, reported by The Hill

statements.text: We are in a race with China and I think there’s huge upside, obviously, with AI as well. There are a lot of benefits to society along with some risks.
statements.venue: Remarks to reporters, reported by The Hill

statements.text: These entities need to be self-sufficient. They ought to be able to take care of their own utilities, their own power, and that ought to be a given any place they go in the country. But they shouldn’t be going places where there isn’t support for them at the local level.
statements.venue: South Dakota TV interview, reported by NOTUS

statements.text: I do think that the threats are real,
I think you have to have at least some sort of a plan and some guardrails around it, which is what I think our bill does,
We are continuing to have those conversations up here on whether or not we can come up with some sort of a legislative framework that would codify some safety protections too,

That’s controversial, as you know, [...] So, I mean, I think the White House is working with senators and House members for that matter to try and come up with something that works but preserves states’ rights.
